name: Muscle dysmorphia (bigorexia)

lead: Muscle dysmorphia is a subtype of body dysmorphic disorder in which a person believes their body is too small or not muscular enough, even when they are already muscular. It is often called bigorexia or reverse anorexia, and is reported more among gym members, bodybuilders and anabolic steroid users.

In looksmaxxing and fitness communities the term comes up in discussions of size, leanness and perceived smallness. Researchers describe it as a recognised clinical condition rather than a lifestyle approach.

paras: Clinicians describe a distorted perception of one's own muscularity driving compulsive training, dietary rules, overtraining and sometimes use of performance-enhancing drugs. Reported risk factors include steroid use, trauma, bullying, perfectionism, low self-esteem and exposure to idealised muscular bodies.

Reported consequences include co-occurring eating, mood, anxiety and substance use disorders, social avoidance, injury from overtraining, and in adolescents a proposed cardiovascular strain. Treatment research is limited, mostly case reports; family-based therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy and SSRIs have some supporting evidence according to Wikipedia's summary.

lead: Muscle dysmorphia, popularly called bigorexia, megarexia or reverse anorexia, is a subtype of body dysmorphic disorder in which people believe their bodies are too small or insufficiently muscular despite often being large or muscular [1]. The DSM-5 classifies it under body dysmorphic disorder and ICD-11 lists it as a subtype; some researchers have proposed treating it as an eating disorder or behavioural addiction [1].

Prevalence estimates vary widely, from about 1% to 54% of men in different studied groups, with higher rates among gym members, weightlifters, bodybuilders and steroid users [1]. A cross-sectional study of 384 male bodybuilders found 5.7% reported muscle dysmorphia, with younger age and protein powder use associated with higher scores, and higher muscle dysmorphia associated with higher social physique anxiety [2].

A journal of athletic training review described the psychobehavioural characteristics of the condition, how to recognise it and treatment and referral options [3]. A 2026 review proposes that bigorexia-related behaviours may be linked to early cardiovascular injury in adolescents [4]. No clinical trials of treatments specific to the condition are cited in these sources; evidence consists largely of case reports [1].
infobox: About 1% to 54% of men in studied groups

paras: The defining feature is a belief that one's body is too small or insufficiently muscular [1]. Commonly described features include excessive muscle-building, dietary restriction or rigid diets, overtraining, use of growth-enhancing drugs, spending more than three hours a day thinking about muscularity, wearing layered clothing to look bigger, and avoiding situations that might expose perceived flaws [1]. About half of affected people lack insight that their perception is unrealistic [1].

The condition was first conceptualised in the late 1990s, initially as an inverse of anorexia nervosa and later linked to body dysmorphic disorder [1]. Co-occurring eating, mood, anxiety and substance use disorders are reported, and suicide attempt rates are described as high [1].

Reported risk factors include anabolic steroid use, trauma such as sexual assault, domestic violence or bullying, low self-esteem, vulnerable narcissism, perfectionism, involvement in sports where size gives an edge, and minority stress among sexual minority men [1]. Wikipedia notes that internalising idealised muscular male bodies in media is a strong predictor of muscularity pursuit among college-aged men [1]. A 2026 study used machine learning to examine gendered stereotypes and body image concerns on diet and fitness online forums [5].

A Spanish study of 141 male gym users in Alicante aged 18 to 45 who wanted to increase muscle mass analysed their body mass index and 24-hour diet and assessed muscle dysmorphia with the Muscle Appearance Satisfaction Scale [6].

Research on treatment is limited, mainly case reports, and no protocol has been validated [1]. Family-based therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy and SSRIs have some supporting evidence [1]. The athletic training review discusses recognition and referral options for athletes and clinicians [3].

Observational and cross-sectional studies exist: a study of 384 male bodybuilders linked higher muscle dysmorphia scores to younger age, protein powder use and social physique anxiety [2], and a Spanish gym-user study examined diets in men screened for the condition [6]. A 2026 review proposes a cardiovascular framework for adolescent bigorexia [4]. No randomised trials of treatments are cited here.

Terms such as bigorexia appear in gym and appearance communities in discussions of 'smallness', bulking and steroid use. Looksmaxxing, which Wikipedia describes as a manosphere practice focused on male attractiveness, has been criticised by commentators for links to body dysmorphia [7].
